content: The target population for tuberculosis (TB) interventions includes sick children and adolescents under the age of 15 who seek care at district hospitals or primary healthcare (PHC) facilities, either through outpatient department visits or systematic TB screening. This also includes children under 15 identified with presumptive TB through routine clinical assessments or systematic screening at these healthcare levels. Patient-level interventions implemented include systematic TB screening, clinical evaluations, testing of nasopharyngeal aspirates (NPA) and stool (or expectorated sputum) using the Xpert Ultra diagnostic tool, optimized chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation using digital radiography, improved reading skills, simplified tools, quality control measures, and treatment decision-making. Health system-level interventions included decentralization strategies. At the district hospital level, this involved implementing a childhood TB diagnostic approach and systematic TB screening at PHC facilities, with referrals to district hospitals. At the PHC level, the strategy included systematic TB screening, clinical evaluations, and testing of NPA and stool (or sputum) using the Ultra diagnostic tool. Feedback from healthcare implementers highlighted that systematic TB screening was perceived as important but challenging to implement, particularly at district hospitals due to high workloads and patient flow. Screening questions were sometimes difficult for parents to understand, especially in crowded waiting areas or in contexts where TB stigma exists. Stool collection and NPA using battery-operated mucus aspirators were feasible and well-accepted at both district hospitals and PHC levels. However, NPA collection often required at least two people (a healthcare worker and a colleague or the child’s parent). Stool samples were frequently not obtained during the child’s visit due to logistical and financial constraints for parents to return with stool containers. Xpert Ultra testing using the battery-operated GeneXpert Edge platform was implemented in all PHC facilities across six countries, with stool samples tested at district hospitals. However, poor sample transport conditions (e.g., long distances, difficult terrain, heavy rain, and challenges maintaining storage temperatures) and power instability at district hospitals and PHC levels negatively impacted stool sample testing. Digitization and transfer of CXR images for clinician access were challenging in several countries, particularly at the PHC level, due to poor internet connectivity. Both decentralization models faced structural and organizational constraints, including issues with human resource availability, stability, and motivation (e.g., frequent staff rotations and transfers, and the need for incentives for additional workloads). Supportive supervision helped address many operational challenges. Clinical mentoring increased clinicians’ confidence in TB diagnosis, including clinical and CXR interpretation skills. In Uganda, a project implemented between 2015 and 2016 focused on decentralizing TB healthcare services for children from tertiary to PHC facilities. This included establishing linkages to support community-based household contact screening and management. District-level trainers were trained in childhood TB management and subsequently trained frontline health workers at PHC facilities through a two-day didactic training enhanced with case studies. Community health workers (CHWs) were trained to screen household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases, refer symptomatic contacts for further evaluation, and provide health education and adherence support for TB preventive treatment (TPT). Post-training mentorship and supportive supervision were conducted monthly for the first three months and then quarterly. Health system strengthening included repairing faulty microscopes, retraining laboratory personnel, training staff in supply chain management, and procuring additional isoniazid supplies. Quarterly data reviews were conducted to assess facility and community performance, identify challenges, and share best practices. The study demonstrated that TB diagnosis and treatment, including clinical diagnosis, can be achieved at the PHC level. Stakeholder engagement, including the National TB Program (NTP), and resources such as skilled personnel, training tools, and financial support, are critical for sustainability and scalability. CHWs can successfully provide integrated care for household contacts of TB cases, including detection and referral of symptomatic child contacts. Linking household contacts with PHC facilities through CHWs can achieve high rates of TPT uptake and completion. In Ethiopia, a high TB burden country, a project implemented between 2016 and 2017 incorporated a TB case management flowchart into the national Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) chart booklet. This included adding a TB screening column to the IMNCI treatment register and providing sensitization training on pediatric TB for child health and TB program officers, health extension supervisors, and facility administrators. Pediatric TB desk references, contact investigation and preventive treatment registers, and updated IMNCI registers were supplied. On-site coaching was provided for specimen collection using nasogastric aspiration techniques. Monitoring of implementation was conducted monthly and quarterly, with periodic performance review meetings. The project demonstrated that childhood TB services, including sample collection, can be decentralized to the PHC level using IMNCI platforms with additional intervention packages. Awareness creation and counseling on the benefits of TPT and management of medication side effects can increase TPT uptake. Strengthening linkages between health facilities and the community through existing platforms is crucial for creating TB awareness, contact investigation, tracing individuals who interrupt treatment, and adherence counseling. In many high TB burden countries, a significant proportion of missing TB cases, including children, seek treatment from private providers or other care providers not linked to the public sector. The private sector is often the first point of care for children presenting with common illnesses such as cough, fever, and diarrhea, especially in countries with a large private healthcare sector. Engaging private providers systematically has increased case detection and improved treatment outcomes. The 2018 WHO Roadmap emphasizes fostering functional partnerships to optimize TB care, including with the private sector. Engaging private healthcare providers aims to improve access to TB care and treatment for individuals who prefer private settings, including children and adolescents. This approach can save patients money by facilitating referrals to free NTP services or enabling privately managed patients to benefit from program-procured medicines, diagnostics, and social support. It also relieves the NTP of some responsibilities in TB care and treatment, such as awareness creation, systematic screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation, and follow-up. The 2018 WHO Public–Private Mix for TB Prevention and Care Roadmap outlines key actions for successful private sector engagement. These include understanding patient preferences and private sector dynamics, setting ambitious public–private mix targets, advocating for political commitment and investment, allocating adequate funding, partnering with intermediaries and stakeholders, and establishing supportive policy and regulatory frameworks.
